newsitem.title: FRANCE: Frenchman guilty of poisoning girl in love mix-up.
newsitem.headline: Frenchman guilty of poisoning girl in love mix-up.

text.p: A French court sentenced a man to 20 years in jail on Sunday for killing a nine-year-old girl who drank cyanide he had intended for his mistress's husband.

The jury in Rouen, northern France, found Jean-Marc Deperrois, the director of a chemical company, guilty of lacing Emilie Tanay's antibiotic with cyanide in June 1994. She died hours after taking the drug.

Deperrois, 46, insisted throughout the three-week trial that he was innocent of the charges of poisoning Emilie's medicine in the mistaken belief it was a drug used by Jean-Michel Tocqueville, the husband of his mistress Sylvie.
His lawyer said he would lodge an appeal after a trial that grabbed nationwide attention and often eclipsed campaigning for the first round of France's parliamentary election on Sunday.
Sylvie Tocqueville was at home in the northern port of Le Havre looking after Emilie the night she died. The girl was rushed to hospital and died in an emergency ward.
The jury handed down its verdict shortly after midnight on Sunday, following a four-hour deliberation. When the verdict was read out, the court erupted into protests from supporters of Deperrois.
"The jurors didn't understand anything. He's innocent," Deperrois' wife Anne-Marie said after the trial. The defendant's two sons, Florent and Fabrice, also stood firmly by him throughout the trial.
Defence lawyer Charles Libman said prosecution evidence was circumstantial at best even though Deperrois had lied by initially denying he possessed cyanide.
Libman said one possibility was that Emilie was accidentally killed by cyanide in an anti-mole poison in her parents' house.
The sentence was lighter than the 25 years requested by the public prosecutor, which itself was less than the maximum life sentence the prosecutor could have sought.
France abolished the death penalty in 1981.

Rhone-Poulenc, the pharmaceutical company that manufactures Josacine, the girl's antibiotic for respiratory tract infections, had the drug pulled off the shelves after she died to check samples, and advised customers to return bottles.
